places.name: Santa Ana Zoo's 50 monkeys
places.text: Right beside the freeway, in Prentice Park, is the Santa Ana Zoo, which opened on March 8, 1952. Joseph Prentice gave the city the land in 1949 on the condition that the zoo keep at least 50 monkeys at all times. It keeps more than a dozen kinds of primates, and it focuses on the animals and plants of Central and South America.
places.more: The 20-acre zoo, owned by the city, draws more than 270,000 visitors a year. Its walk-through Colors of the Amazon Aviary, opened in 1996, is lushly planted, with winding streams and South American birds. Giant anteaters, rheas and guanacos live in Tierra de las Pampas, the Land of the Grasses. One of the most popular rides is the Zoofari Express, a children's train. Its first engine, built in 1954, ran for 44 years at Santa's Village in Sky Forest, and when that park closed in 1998, the zoo's friends group bought the train and volunteers restored it. In 2017, with the monkey habitats outdated, the Association of Zoos and Aquariums declined to accredit the zoo. It regained accreditation in 2025, the same year River's Edge opened, a reworked home for howler monkeys, spider monkeys and tamarins.

places.name: Angel Stadium and the Big A
places.text: East of the freeway, near Katella Avenue, is Angel Stadium, home of the Los Angeles Angels since 1966. Among major league ballparks still in use, only Fenway Park, Wrigley Field and Dodger Stadium are older. From 1980 to 1994 the Los Angeles Rams played football here too. At the edge of the parking lot, beside Highway 57, stands the Big A, a 230-foot sign with a halo near the top.
places.more: Founded in 1961, the Angels were the first major league baseball team to start out in California rather than move there, and they spent four seasons at Dodger Stadium before coming to Anaheim. The 210-ton Big A first held up the scoreboard in left field. When the stands were enlarged and enclosed for the Rams, it was moved 1,300 feet to the parking lot. For years its halo blinked after dark when the Angels won; since at least 2023 it stays lit, shining brighter after a win. The 1994 Northridge earthquake dropped a giant video screen onto upper-deck seats before dawn, and no one was hurt. At the main entrance stand two giant Angels caps, and the tag on one gives its size as 649 and a half.

places.name: Downtown Los Angeles skyline
places.text: The towers of downtown Los Angeles rise to the west, across the Los Angeles River. The one with a thin spire on top is the Wilshire Grand Center, finished in 2017. Counting the spire it stands 1,100 feet, the tallest building in the United States west of Chicago, though the U.S. Bank Tower's roof is higher. Many towers around it have flat tops because a 1974 city fire rule required rooftop helipads on tall buildings.
places.more: Between the towers and the river, a little over a mile west of the freeway, is El Pueblo, near where the city was founded in 1781. By one historian's count, only two of the 44 founding settlers were white, and 26 had some African ancestry. Its Avila Adobe, built in 1818 with a roof sealed by tar from the La Brea Tar Pits, is the oldest house still standing in the city. A campaign to save it led to Olvera Street, which opened on Easter Sunday 1930 as a Mexican marketplace. On the east side of the freeway, near the I-10 junction, stands the old County General Hospital, an Art Deco giant of 1933 nicknamed the Great Stone Mother, which once held 3,000 beds. A hospital earthquake safety law passed after the 1994 Northridge earthquake left it out of compliance, and its replacement nearby was renamed LA General in 2023.
places.spot: Look for a tall downtown tower topped by a thin spire.

places.name: The 1933 Griffith Park fire
places.text: On October 3, 1933, a brush fire in Griffith Park killed at least 29 men who volunteered or were ordered to fight it. Thousands of workers on a federally funded project were in the park that day, clearing brush and building trails for 40 cents an hour. The fire burned only about 47 acres, yet for 85 years it was the deadliest wildfire in California history.
places.more: It started a little after 2 in the afternoon in a pile of debris in Mineral Wells Canyon, in the hills west of the freeway. With no piped water nearby, the men beat at the flames with shovels. Foremen who knew nothing about fighting fires set ill-judged backfires and sent hundreds of workers into a steep canyon. Firefighters arrived at 2:26 but struggled to work around thousands of untrained people. At about 3 o'clock the wind shifted, and the fire rushed up Dam Canyon, jumped a hastily dug firebreak and overtook the workers, injuring more than 100. Record keeping was so poor that it took weeks to count the dead. The courts ruled the victims could not be compensated, because they had been hired informally, and the memorial plaque placed at the park entrance can no longer be found.

places.name: Burbank, the Media Capital
places.text: Burbank, which the freeway passes through, is commonly known as the Media Capital of the World. Warner Bros. and the Walt Disney Company both have their headquarters here, in the Media District, a couple of miles west of the freeway. Warner Bros. took over the First National studio lot in 1928, and Disney, after the success of Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, finished its Burbank studio on Buena Vista Street in 1939.
places.more: Most of Casablanca's major scenes were shot on Stage 1 at Warner Bros. in 1942. Because wartime rules banned filming near airports, even its foggy airport scene was made on the stage. Walt Disney first hoped to build a Mickey Mouse Park beside his studio, but his aides said the land was too small, and one city council member told him, We don't want the carny atmosphere in Burbank. He built Disneyland in Anaheim instead. NBC's former studios here taped The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson, and the comedy show Laugh-In made a running joke of beautiful downtown Burbank. Warner Bros. runs public backlot tours, while Disney is the only major studio that does not.

places.name: The Brink's jewelry heist
places.text: At 2 in the morning on July 11, 2022, a Brink's tractor-trailer carrying jewelry from a show in San Mateo to one in Pasadena pulled into a truck stop at the Frazier Mountain Park Road exit. One guard went inside to eat while the other slept in the cab. Within 27 minutes, thieves cut the trailer's padlock and made off with about two dozen of its 73 bags of jewelry.
places.more: Brink's put the loss at 8.7 million dollars, based on the values the jewelers had declared. But some jewelers admitted in depositions that they routinely listed less than the true value to keep insurance costs down, and some estimates reach 100 million dollars, which would make it one of the largest jewelry thefts in modern American history. Each bag weighed 70 to 100 pounds, so moving that many so fast suggests several thieves, and since most of the missing bags came from the front of the trailer, they seemed to know which ones they wanted. The trailer was secured with just a padlock and a plastic seal. Brink's and the jewelers sued each other, and some jewelers lost their businesses. In 2025 federal prosecutors indicted seven Los Angeles area men accused of following delivery trucks and stealing from them at truck stops, and some of the jewelry was recovered.

places.name: Valley fever in the dust
places.text: The soils of the San Joaquin Valley, especially its southern end, can hold Coccidioides, a fungus that causes valley fever, also called San Joaquin Valley fever. Its spores rise into the air when dusty ground is stirred up by wind, farming or construction, and people catch it by breathing them in. It is not contagious, and about 60 percent of people who are infected have few or no symptoms.
places.more: It follows a pattern called grow and blow: the fungus grows in the soil after rain, then dry, windy weather lifts its spores. Cases have been climbing. Kern County recorded about 1,000 in 2014 and 3,000 in 2021, and California reported nearly 12,500 cases in 2024, the most the state has documented. Most people who get sick have symptoms like bronchitis or pneumonia that clear up in a few weeks, and serious disease develops in fewer than 5 percent of those infected, mostly people with weakened immune systems. Farm and construction workers face more risk, and so do dogs, which dig and sniff at the ground. In 2005, two state prisons on the West Side, near Coalinga and Avenal, had rates of at least 3,000 cases per 100,000 people. The CDC advises avoiding dusty places and, during dust storms, staying inside with the windows closed.

places.name: The farm water signs
places.text: Starting around 2008, big signs went up in fields along I-5, with slogans like Congress Created Dust Bowl and No Water Equals No Jobs. Many came from Families Protecting the Valley, a loosely organized group of San Joaquin Valley farmers and other locals. Russ Waymire, a Hanford real estate broker and former farmer, put up its first sign with a friend's help, and farmers soon offered their land for more.
places.more: Farmers say federal rules meant to protect smelt and salmon have cut their water. In June 2011 the Associated Press reported several hundred new signs along I-5 and Highway 99, with lines like Man-made drought and Food grows where water flows. Farmers with the newest federal water contracts are the first to face cuts, the report noted, which is why West Side farmers got the least water during that drought. It also cited a Congressional Research Service report finding that less than a quarter of the cuts in supply came from endangered species protections, and that most came from the drought itself. Environmentalists said the signs gave a false picture of the drought and its causes. The group was founded in 2000 by Denis Prosperi, a Madera almond and wine grape farmer, and in 2015 it ran solely on donations.

places.name: Sacramento, the state capital
places.text: Sacramento has been California's capital since 1854. The new state's lawmakers first met in San Jose, moved to Vallejo in 1852 and to Benicia in 1853, and then settled here. The State Capitol downtown, less than a mile east of the freeway, was modeled on the U.S. Capitol. It was begun in 1860 and finished in 1874, and lawmakers moved into its chambers in 1869 while work went on around them.
places.more: Around the Capitol, Capitol Park spreads over 40 acres, with more than 200 kinds of trees and 155 memorials. Right beside the freeway, at Second and J streets in Old Sacramento, stands the B. F. Hastings Building, a plain two-story brick building from 1852. In 1860 and 1861 it was the western end of the Pony Express, whose relays of riders carried mail to and from St. Joseph, Missouri, more than 1,800 miles away. The service lasted only 18 months before the telegraph replaced it. The building was also the first home of the California Supreme Court, and today it holds a Wells Fargo history museum. Sacramento itself is the oldest incorporated city in California, dating to February 27, 1850.

places.name: Yellow-billed magpie
places.text: Watch the fields and tall trees along here for the yellow-billed magpie, a black-and-white bird with a bright yellow bill and a small patch of yellow skin around each eye. It lives only in California, in the Central Valley and the foothills and mountains beside it. In good light its black feathers shine green, blue or purple.
places.more: Magpies belong to the crow family, and these are social birds that roost together. When one dies, others gather around it and call loudly for 10 to 15 minutes, a kind of funeral. Pairs build dome-shaped nests of sticks and mud high in tall trees, sometimes far out on long branches to keep predators away. They eat mostly insects, especially grasshoppers, plus acorns, fruit and carrion. West Nile virus hit them hard: between 2004 and 2006, about half of all yellow-billed magpies are thought to have died of it. The IUCN now lists the species as vulnerable, though it is still common in many places.
places.spot: Look for a black-and-white bird with a yellow beak.

places.name: Ishi and the Yahi
places.text: The foothill canyons east of here, along Mill and Deer creeks, are the ancestral homeland of the Yahi, the southernmost group of the Yana people. After the Gold Rush, settlers killed nearly all of the Yahi; in 1865, about 40 were killed in the Three Knolls Massacre on Mill Creek. A few survivors hid in the canyons for decades. The last known Yahi, a man the world came to call Ishi, walked out near Oroville in 1911, starving and alone.
places.more: Ishi means man in the Yana language. Anthropologist Alfred Kroeber gave him the name, because Yahi custom kept a person from speaking his own name until another Yahi introduced him, and none were left. University of California anthropologists took him to their museum in San Francisco, where he worked as a janitor, showed how he made bows and stone arrowheads, and was recorded singing and telling stories on 148 wax cylinders. He died of tuberculosis in 1916. His brain was sent to the Smithsonian, which returned it in 2000 to Yana descendants in the Redding Rancheria and the Pit River Tribe. The 41,339-acre Ishi Wilderness, about 20 miles east of Red Bluff, protects canyons believed to be his people's ancestral grounds, and the 2024 Park Fire burned nearly all of it.

places.name: Cottonwood truck scales
places.text: The truck scales here are the Cottonwood Commercial Vehicle Enforcement Facility, run by the California Highway Patrol. Officers and inspectors check trucks and their drivers against North American safety standards and state law. The first station, on one side of the freeway, opened in 2000, and a second, for trucks going the other way, opened in 2025.
places.more: Big rigs also travel slower than cars by law. California limits trucks with three or more axles, and every vehicle towing a trailer, to 55 miles an hour, even where cars may go 70, as on parts of rural I-5. At weigh stations, some scales weigh trucks while they keep rolling, while older scales make them stop, and signal lights tell each driver whether to pull in for a closer look or return to the highway. Staff here are also trained to spot impaired drivers, stolen vehicles and human trafficking. The station sits in the rolling grass and oak hills of Tehama County, about 2 miles south of Cottonwood Creek, the Shasta County line.
places.spot: Look for the truck scale station beside the freeway.

places.name: Gray wolves return
places.text: Gray wolves have returned to Siskiyou County. In late December 2011, a collared wolf from Oregon known as OR-7 crossed the state line, the first wild wolf confirmed in California since 1924. In 2015 a trail camera in Siskiyou County confirmed the Shasta Pack, two adults and five pups, the state's first resident wolf pack in more than a century.
places.more: OR-7, nicknamed Journey, had wandered more than 1,000 miles from the Wallowa Mountains of northeastern Oregon, and in 2012 he roamed across seven counties of northeastern California. The Shasta Pack's breeding female was his sister, and the pack later vanished, for reasons no one has explained. In 2021 another Oregon wolf, OR-85, and a female formed the Whaleback Pack in Siskiyou County, and seven pups were confirmed that September. By December 2025 the state counted 55 wolves in nine packs. Wolves are listed as endangered in California, and the state has set aside money to pay ranchers for livestock lost to them. In 2025, after nearly 100 tries at scaring them off, state wildlife officials killed four wolves from a Plumas County pack that kept preying on cattle, the first time the state had done so.

places.name: Agricultural inspection at Hornbrook
places.text: Traffic entering California on I-5 stops here, near Hornbrook, at one of 16 agricultural inspection stations that the California Department of Food and Agriculture runs where major highways cross into the state. Inspectors look for pests in plants or cargo that could harm California's farms. Passenger cars with California or neighboring-state plates usually get just a few questions about what they carry.
places.more: RVs, commercial trucks, and vehicles hauling boats or livestock count as higher risk, and their loads may be looked over. Loads of beehives are logged, and the driver must name where in California the bees are going, so that county's agriculture office can inspect them on arrival. The first stations went up in the early 1920s on highways from Nevada near Reno, after destructive alfalfa weevils turned up in campgrounds along them, and in the first year inspectors found live weevils inside camping gear. Together the stations stop about 27 million vehicles a year, and the state says each dollar spent on them saves 14 dollars in pest losses. Inspectors cannot make arrests, but they can hold someone until the Highway Patrol arrives.
places.spot: Look for the inspection station where traffic entering California stops.
